entries.seminar_title: Foundations of Robust Optimization: Divergence Preferences
entries.speaker: Tommaso Denti
entries.abstract: We study a decision maker who, like a subjective expected utility maximizer, uses a reference probability model to assess the likelihood of different states of the world, but worries that the model may be misspecified. They evaluate each choice by minimizing expected utility over alternative models, with a penalty for departures from the reference model. We characterize the preferences that arise when these departures are measured by a statistical divergence. Under these preferences, choices are ranked solely by the distributions of outcomes they induce under the reference model. When two outcome distributions are equally attractive, the decision maker weakly prefers either one to any mixture of the two. We interpret this property as aversion to model misspecification. In two economic examples, we connect this aversion to the informativeness principle in moral hazard problems and show how it can give rise to a winner’s curse in first-price auctions.
entries.bio: Tommaso Denti is an Assistant Professor of Economics at NYU Stern Business.

entries.seminar_title: Skin Tone and Racial Inequality in the US: Evidence from the 20th Century
entries.speaker: Kamelia Stavreva
entries.abstract: Empirical work on racial inequality typically relies on a binary Black–white comparison, treating racial categories as uniform and masking meaningful variation in how individuals are treated within groups. Using newly collected WWII draft registration records containing information on skin tone for the near universe of men born between 1898–1929, linked to the 1940 Census, we document large intra-racial disparities by skin color. Black men with light skin earn about 37% more than their darker-skinned peers. This unconditional gap is economically significant—if all Black men earned what light-skinned Black men did, the Black–white earnings gap in 1940 would be roughly 18% smaller. We explore several mechanisms behind these disparities. Comparing brothers raised in the same household, family fixed effects eliminate essentially the entire education gap, yet darker-skinned brothers still earn about 10% less (9 log points), roughly a quarter of the unconditional gap in the sibling sample, pointing to a labor market penalty distinct from the categorical disadvantages tied to racial classification. We then consider the role of discriminatory institutions. While Jim Crow exposure depresses educational attainment for Black men overall, we find no differential impact by skin tone, consistent with the one-drop rule’s uniform legal treatment. Finally, we follow men from 1940 to 1950 and find that among men in the same 1940 occupation, lighter-skinned men were more likely to move into skilled work. Exploiting WWII-driven variation in labor market tightness, we find that shocks that reduced Black–white inequality had no detectable differential effect by skin tone. Our results show that differences in outcomes by skin tone represent a distinct form of inequality, one that reflects both inherited disadvantage and discriminatory forces that sort Black men by color and appear to differ from those driving broader Black-white inequality.
entries.bio: Kamelia Stavreva is a PhD Student in Economics at Columbia University.

entries.seminar_title: Integrity and Unraveling in Carbon Offset Markets
entries.speaker: Anna Russo
entries.abstract: Carbon offset markets aim to lower abatement costs through trade, but when adverse selection drives a wedge between credits and true carbon reductions, enforcing unbiased trade—counting credits only for expected reductions—may unravel the market. We investigate this tension in tropical forest offsets. Credits exceed reductions by an order of magnitude. A natural experiment provides direct evidence of unraveling: when a standardized contract pooled heterogeneous credits at a single price, prices fell, adverse selection worsened, and trade collapsed. Yet, buyers value nominal credits beyond their underlying carbon reductions. An equilibrium model of land use, crediting, and demand shows that this demand acts as an implicit subsidy, sustaining trade that adverse selection would otherwise unravel, but with small, vastly overstated abatement. Under unbiased trade, the market unravels even at high carbon prices, despite socially valuable abatement opportunities. Preserving both trade and environmental integrity would require a profound change in market design, substantial subsidies, and major improvements in baseline measurement. Without this, gains from offset trade may not be realizable.
entries.bio: Anna Russo is an Assistant Professor of Economics and Social Studies at Harvard University.
